Introduction The NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide, PMS 437 (FBFRG) contains helpful references to the factors from the fire triangle (fuels, weather, and topography), including features that are vital to fieldgoing fire managers. It provides detail about fire behavior models and tools used to estimate probability of ignition, spread/size, fireline intensity, and crown fire potential. The reference material is intended to assist with decision support. This guide will be reviewed annually and updated as needed to reflect the most recent science and technologies used to improve and assist with decision support, fireline safety, and fire behavior interpretation. As new and improved safety zone research is obtained and available for distribution, the FBFRG will be updated. Supporting documentation, including instructional videos, will be uploaded periodically to the official YouTube channel: www.youtube.com/user/FireBehaviorSC. Weather Forecast Confidence Forecast confidence is the analyst's professional judgment about how reliable a given fire behavior forecast is based on the quality and consistency of the inputs used to produce it. It communicates to decision-makers how much trust they should place in the prediction, not just what the prediction says. For applications requiring forecast information with very high confidence or accuracy, the typical Confidence Horizon is approximately three

to produce it. It communicates to decision-makers how much trust they should place in the prediction, not just what the prediction says. For applications requiring forecast information with very high confidence or accuracy, the typical Confidence Horizon is approximately three days. However, this horizon is not fixed; shifts in forecast skill routinely expand or contract the period during which very high confidence is achievable, thereby changing the Confidence Horizon. Figure 1. Typical forecast Confidence Horizon. Understanding these shifts is especially important when selecting an appropriate fire behavior modeling tool, applying forecast data within that tool, and documenting assumptions made during analysis. The atmosphere is chaotic, but sometimes there is rhythm in the chaos. Climate outlook scientists study coupled oceanic and atmospheric forcing mechanisms-such as El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle and Madden Julian Oscillation (MJO)-that influence several teleconnection or long-range, longterm correlated weather patterns that determine meteorological impacts across North America. Forecast skill typically increases (i.e., rhythm in the chaos) for mid- and long-range outlooks when certain forcing mechanisms and teleconnection patterns align. During these periods, the normal NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 1 of 205

Confidence Horizon may extend, allowing monthly or seasonal outlooks to carry medium-to occasionally high-confidence for general weather patterns such as warmer and drier conditions and sometimes frequent wind events. This represents a shift from the typically Low to Very Low confidence associated with longer-range forecasts. Other teleconnection alignments can produce mixed atmospheric forcing signals, thus leading to unusually Low confidence periods (e.g., no rhythm). Forecast Models Meteorologists produce weather forecasts primarily by interpreting and validating weather prediction models. Several models are available with varying update frequencies, output intervals, temporal ranges, and spatial resolutions. These models are periodically refined as new research, observing techniques, and increased computing capabilities emerge. No singular model is perfect. Forecast models are classified into deterministic, ensemble and convective-allowing models (CAM). Models may be global, regional, or limited to small areas. High resolution models (≤ 5 km) generally fall into the CAM category. CAM operate on smaller areas with 15-minute to 1 hour time-steps and can account for data-intensive convection modeling. They can resolve terrain-induced and altered wind patterns, small-scale boundary passages and banded and cellular precipitation features. Due to the differing scales, physics, and initial conditions, CAMs models can produce widely varying solutions, making it challenging for forecasters to determine which scenario is most likely. Fireline Observations Location and Timing of Fireline Weather Observations There are four key observation times within a 24-hour period that are valuable for assessing forecasts and evaluating thresholds associated with fire behavior transitions: * Early morning observations that capture minimum temperature and maximum humidity. * Late afternoon observations that capture maximum temperature and minimum humidity occur. * Times when active fire behavior increases or diminishes during the burn period. * Hourly observations throughout the afternoon, or whenever conditions change, may be requested by fireline supervisors, or as needed to maintain situational awareness. Selecting an Appropriate Observation Site The weather observer should select observation sites that most accurately represent environmental conditions around the fire. Consider the following: * Determine whether a ridgetop, midslope, or drainage bottom location is most representative. * On slopes, account for aspect and slope steepness. * Identify a fuel bed representative of fire conditions. Do not take observations in nonrepresentative areas such as near bodies of water (with exceptions, as needed), on roads, in the burned area, or next to parked vehicles. * Ideally, choose a safe site upwind or on the flank of the fire. Generally, ventilated areas in the shade are desirable locations for the

Generally, ventilated areas in the shade are desirable locations for the observation. * Minimize effects of the fire on your observation and avoid observations affected by gusty indraft flows and radiant heat from the fireline. Note the Type of Instruments Used Indicate whether observations were taken with an electronic weather sensor or traditional sling psychrometer. Electronic temperature and humidity sensors should be regularly calibrated against reliable instruments or by following calibration instructions from the manufacturer's website. Batteries should be checked frequently. Communicate and Document the Weather Observation Weather observations are only useful if communicated promptly and accurately to personnel who need it. Report current observations over the radio to maintain situational awareness. * Follow established procedures for periodic radio reports to fireline supervisors or the incident communications unit. * Report measurements with trends, such as "Temperature: 75 degrees, up 5 degrees from last hour." Temperature, Relative Humidity, and Vapor Pressure Deficit Observations Estimating temperature, relative humidity (RH), and dewpoint can provide insight into critical fire behavior thresholds related to probability of ignition and crown fire potential. Using Sling Psychrometers The following steps outline how to obtain wet- and dry- bulb temperatures using a sling psychrometer: * If the psychrometer has been in your pack, hang it in a tree or shaded area to let it adjust to the outside air temperature. This may be a good time to take the wind observation. * Stand in a shaded, open area away with enough space to whirl the instrument without striking any objects. In open terrain, use your body shade to shade the psychrometer. Whenever possible, take observations over a fuel bed that is representative of the fuels involved in the fire. Avoid heat sinks such as black pavement, or extensive areas of rock. * Face the wind to prevent body heat from influencing the thermometers. * Saturate the wick of the wet bulb with clean, mineral free water (distilled, if available) at air temperature. * Ventilate thermometers by whirling at full arm's length, arm parallel to the ground, for one minute. * After one minute,

* Saturate the wick of the wet bulb with clean, mineral free water (distilled, if available) at air temperature. * Ventilate thermometers by whirling at full arm's length, arm parallel to the ground, for one minute. * After one minute, read the wet bulb temperature. Whirl for another 40 to 50 times and read again. Continue this process until the wet-bulb temperature stops decreasing. Record the lowest value. If the wet bulb is not read at the lowest point, the calculated RH will be too high. * Read the dry bulb temperature immediately after obtaining the lowest wet bulb temperature. * Determine the RH using the psychrometric tables. Calculate dewpoint each time as significant variation may indicate an inaccurate observation. Important Tips - Beginners may produce inaccurate psychrometer readings due to the following common mistakes: * Switching psychrometers from one observation to the next. Use the same sling throughout. * Not spinning/ventilating the psychrometer long enough to reach equilibrium. * Not wetting the wick enough or allowing it dry. * Holding the instrument too close to the body or taking too long to read the thermometers. * Touching the bulb ends while reading. * Not facing into the wind. Calculating Vapor Pressure Deficit Used extensively in greenhouse and agricultural applications, VPD is a strong indicator of green vegetation moisture stress. The Growing Season Index (GSI) incorporates VPD as a key criterion to green-up and curing phenology, with values around 9 mb (millibars) considered optimal for plant growth. While RH expresses the amount of water vapor (moisture) in the air as a percentage of saturation, VPD measures the absolute difference between the actual moisture and the amount it could hold at saturation. Potentially counter-intuitive to RH, VPD increases as the moisture deficit increases and generally follows a seasonal trend, low in winter and higher in warm summer months, driven by variation in temperature and atmospheric humidity. VPD provides important insight about the role of ambient temperature and atmospheric humidity. * At low temperatures, even low RH does not produce a high VPD. * At high temperatures, the same low RH can result in a much higher VPD, indicating a stronger drying potential. RH does not produce a high VPD. * At high temperatures, the same low RH can result in a much higher VPD, indicating a stronger drying potential. Figure 3 provides an example of interpreting VPD. Colors depict potential for extreme fire behavior: green indicates optimal plant growth conditions, but as the temperature increases, higher VPD indicates drier air, increased moisture loss from vegetation, and greater potential for extreme fire behavior. Crossover Concept thresholds, where extreme fire behavior exists, are indicated by black boxes on VPD tables. The Crossover Concept The Crossover concept, introduced by the Alberta Forest Service (1985), is a fire weather indicator used to identify potentially critical burning conditions. A "Crossover" occurs when the temperature (in degrees Celsius[C]) exceeds the RH (in %). For example, a temperature of 25°C and a RH of 20% indicates a Crossover situation. Crossover conditions indicate a high potential for fire ignition and rapid spread, especially when combined with wind. The Crossover point is significant because it reflects very dry air and fuels, making it a valuable tool for fire managers in anticipating elevated, dangerous fire behavior. An RH 15% at 60°F has a different effect on the fire environment than at 80°F.

Sky Observations Local terrain and other site-specific factors can modify general atmospheric conditions, creating more localized effects. Weather observers provide important information to meteorologists by reporting the visual cues and the timing of changes throughout the day. Visual cues should be recorded in the remarks section of the weather observation to provide a time-stamped reference. Firefighters should pay attention to both the fire weather forecast and the sky for signs of changing or severe conditions that can influence the fire environment. When visual cues are significant, photographs-paired with a photo log noting location, date, time, and other identifiers-can provide valuable supporting documentation. Airport webcams, available at http://airportwebcams.net/airport-webcams-by-time-zone/, can provide useful real-time information. Synoptic (large-scale) forecasts current-condition reports reference the relative stability of the atmosphere. Several indicators of stability are outlined below. In general, a stable atmosphere suppresses strong vertical motion. Cloud build-ups during stable conditions tend to be broad and flat, sometimes spreading across much of the sky. Additionally, stable conditions favor smoke accumulation near the surface, which can moderate fire behavior due to limited NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 17 of 205

winds, lack of solar radiation to heat fuels, reduced temperatures, and higher relative humidities. However, strong general winds can still occur during stable conditions depending upon the overall weather pattern. In contrast, unstable conditions enhance vertical motion and typically increase ventilation around active fires. Lightning and Wind * Report lightning immediately so fireline supervisors can take appropriate safety precautions and meteorologists can review lightning-detection tools. * Sudden wind shifts may indicate a breaking inversion or frontal passage. Indicators of Stability: Smoke, Dust, and Fire * A rising smoke column signals neutral or unstable conditions, while a flattening smoke column indicates an inversion at that level. * A smoke column that changes direction as it rises indicates wind shear or influence from local winds. * A smoke column that develops a pyrocumulus cap cloud indicates strong instability and the potential for downdrafts. * Haze and reduced visibility often indicator inversions. Determine whether the inversion is local (e.g., nighttime) or more general and persistent throughout the day. If haze or poor visibility lifts during the burn period, expect increased fire behavior. Dust clouds radiating away from thunderstorms indicate potentially dangerous downdrafts. Dust devils indicate surface instability. Firewhirls occur when fire-generated convection interacts with winds, adjacent terrain-generated eddies, instability from cold fronts, and/or multiple interacting fire plumes. The NWCG Fire Weather Cloud Chart, PMS 438, https://www.nwcg.gov/publications/438, provides examples of sky features important for wildland firefighters. Cloud types and formations are valuable indicators of atmospheric stability and potential changes. Clouds That Indicate Instability in the Atmosphere * Cumulus (various types) - Signal weak instability. They are usually not a concern for firefighters, but continued vertical growth should be monitored. Developing cumulus can precede sudden downdrafts and gusty winds. * Altocumulus (various types, including castellanus) - Indicate increasing moisture and instability in the upper atmosphere and a possible upcoming weather change. Altocumulus castellanus in particular indicate increasing moisture and instability with the potential for thunderstorms. * Cumulonimbus - Reflect very unstable conditions. Fully developed, mature thunderstorms contain extreme vertical motion and can produce sudden gusty, erratic winds-sometimes miles away from the cloud buildup. Severe thunderstorms can generate localized wind gusts over 100 mph along with lightning, virga, hail, shelf clouds or even tornadoes. Clearly, cumulonimbus clouds pose many hazards to the firefighter exposed on the fireline. * Pyrocumulus - Very unstable. The four critical weather elements that may produce extreme fire behavior are low RH, strong surface wind, unstable air, and drought. Critical fire weather patterns that support these conditions can be separated into two primary categories: (1) patterns that produce strong surface winds, and (2) patterns that produce atmospheric instability. In both cases, an unusually dry airmass for the region and season must also occur. In brush and timber fuels, drought becomes an important precursor by increasing fuel availability and receptiveness. Most periods of critical fire weather occur in transition zones between high- and low-pressure systems, at both the surface and upper levels. Surface-pressure patterns of most concern are those associated with cold fronts and terrain-driven foehn winds. Cold front passages are important to firefighters because of strong, shifting winds and unstable air that can enhance the smoke column or produce thunderstorms. Foehn winds occur on the lee side of mountain ranges and are typically very strong, warm, and dry, sometimes abruptly so. The region between the upper ridge and upper trough has the most critical upper-air pattern because of unstable air and strong winds that can mix to the surface. Critical Fire Weather Patterns These descriptions include common terminology used by meteorologists to describe critical fire weather patterns. While you will often encounter these terms in NWS Area Forecast Discussion (AFD), https://forecast.weather.gov/product_sites.php?site=CRH&product=AFD), fire weather planning forecasts, and Predictive Service seven-day outlook assessments, other terminology may be used. East of the Rocky Mountains: Critical fire weather patterns are associated with the periphery of high pressure systems, particularly in the pre-frontal and post-frontal areas. In the Northern Plains, Great Lakes, and the Northeastern U.S., pre-frontal high pressure from the Pacific, Northwestern Canada, and Hudson Bay can produce very dry conditions. Cold fronts can produce relatively short-lived but intense periods of strong winds and instability capable of driving extreme fire behavior. Southeastern U.S.: Drought is frequently associated with La Niña state of the southern oscillation pattern or a blocking ridge aloft near the Atlantic coast. Often critical fire weather patterns follow the frontal passage that brings extremely dry air due to a strong westerly or northwesterly flow. Watch for strong winds that

the southern oscillation pattern or a blocking ridge aloft near the Atlantic coast. Often critical fire weather patterns follow the frontal passage that brings extremely dry air due to a strong westerly or northwesterly flow. Watch for strong winds that accompany the flow. Beware of advancing tropical storms that can produce significant wind shifts as well. Southwestern U.S.: Before monsoons develop, the breakdown of the upper ridge produces breezy, dry, unstable surface conditions that often intensify as the ridge collapses. During transition to the monsoon pattern, shallow monsoons can produce gusty wind, low RH, and lightning without much precipitation. Rocky Mountain and Intermountain Regions: The primary pattern is the upper ridge combined with a surface thermal trough that produces a dry and windy surface cold front. Along the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, weather patterns producing Chinook winds bring strong downslope winds that are unusually dry and warm. Thunderstorm Dynamics: Outflows, and Downbursts Thunderstorms near a fire have the potential to generate outflow gust fronts or downbursts, regardless of whether the storm is influenced by the fire. Any sign of precipitation-rain at the surface or virga aloft-indicates the storm has developed enough to produce these types of winds, along with lightning. Outflow gust fronts spread outward from the base of the storm, usually in the direction of storm motion. They occur with all well-developed convection, can last tens of minutes to an hour or more, and can travel tens to hundreds of kilometers. Downbursts are much less common, shorter lived, and affect a much smaller area but can also produce abrupt changes in wind speed and direction. Either type of wind can abruptly change the speed and direction of fire spread. Figure 12. Thunderstorm dynamics. The few hours preceding sea breeze are typically the warmest and driest and coincide with increasing wind speeds and unstable conditions. After the sea breeze front passes, temperatures become cooler while humidity and stability increase.

These patterns are typically associated with an upper ridge and a strong mid-level dry intrusion-two ingredients that often precede the breakdown of the upper ridge pattern. Fire-Slowing or Fire-Stopping Patterns Geographic areas experience fire-slowing and/or fire-stopping periods for three primary reasons: * A partial or widespread change in the weather and fuel regime. * Partial green-up or increased fuel moisture promoted by periods of precipitation. * Temporary changes-such as a cool, moist, stable weather regime replacing hot, dry, and unstable conditions during a multi-day period. Understand that the fire-slowing and/or fire-stopping period is a temporary change. Across the U.S., four main patterns commonly produce fire-slowing or stopping conditions: * Closed low, deep-trough frontal passages * Monsoon bursts * Tropical storms * Smoke events The season-ending period is similar to a fire-slowing period, but the magnitude and duration of change are greater. Estimating Winds for Fire Behavior Definitions Critical Winds dominate the fire environment and can easily override local wind influences. Examples include frontal winds, Foehn winds, thunderstorm outflows, whirlwinds, surfacing or low-level jets (reverse wind profiles), and glacier winds. General (Synoptic-Scale) Winds-such as synoptic scale, gradient, free air, and ridgetop-are largescale winds produced by broad pressure gradients between high- and low-pressure systems. They may be influenced and modified considerably in the lower atmosphere by terrain and vegetative structure. Local (Mesoscale) Winds-such as thermal, convective, drainage, and slope winds-develop from local temperature differences generated over comparatively small areas by local terrain and weather. They differ from synoptic winds because they are confined to near surface and are controlled by the strength

Winds-such as thermal, convective, drainage, and slope winds-develop from local temperature differences generated over comparatively small areas by local terrain and weather. They differ from synoptic winds because they are confined to near surface and are controlled by the strength of the daily solar cycle. * Slope Winds are driven by heat exchange at the slope surface. Upslope winds can begin within minutes of solar heating and are influenced by slope length, steepness, and aspect. Typical speeds range from 3 to 8 mph. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 29 of 205

The transition from upslope to downslope wind begins when slopes enter afternoon shadow and cooling of the surface begins. The transition includes: (1) weakening upslope flow, (2) a period of relative calm, and (3) gentle, laminar downslope flow. Downslope winds are very shallow and at a slower speed than upslope winds, generally 2 to 5 mph. The cooled denser air is stable and the downslope flow, therefore, tends to be laminar. * Valley Winds are linked to slope winds but development lags behind slope winds by 1 to 3 hours. Peak speeds can double those of slope winds, reaching 10 to 15 mph. Land and Sea Breeze Circulations form during the day and can reach 10 to 15 mph during peak solar heating in the afternoon. The nighttime land breeze is lighter, generally 5 to 10 mph. Adjusting Surface (20 foot) Wind to Midflame Wind Speed Once general winds have been adjusted to represent 20-foot surface winds based on terrain and other local factors, the next step is to convert 20-foot wind to midflame wind speed (MFWS). MFWS is the velocity of wind at the mid-height of the flames and is always less than the 20-foot wind speed due to the friction of vegetation closer to the surface. This is why adjustment factors are always less than 1. The adjustment depends on canopy sheltering and surface fuel bed depth. The process involves understanding how the wind is oriented with the terrain, whether the terrain is flat or sloped, and a characterization of the canopy characteristics. Note that the degree of sheltering also varies depending on fire position within terrain features. Adjustment criteria include: For unsheltered fuels, all canopy covers less than 20%, and all crown ratios are less than 0.2. WAF for unsheltered fuel is a function of fuel bed depth only (typically estimated by identifying the fuel model). For sheltered fuels, WAF depends on a combination of canopy cover, canopy height, and average crown ratio for the site. As combinations of these factors increase, WAF transitions from partially sheltered to fully sheltered. Figure 20. Adjusting surface wind for sheltered fuels. Fuels Surface Fuel Model Selection Each surface fuel model is a selection of numerical inputs used in the Rothermel (1972) surface fire spread equation. Fuel model selection guides are useful, but the final choice must be made by the analyst based on experience with fire behavior in the fuel bed being evaluated. Two Sets of Surface Fuel Models This guide integrates the original 13 models with the 40 standard models introduced in 2005. Although the 40 standard models were designed to stand alone, all 53 models are available in current fire modeling systems. While the original 13 models were grouped into only four carrier types, they can be effectively redistributed across the six types defined with the newer models. Consider the objectives that guided the development of these two sets. Even though the newer fuel models have been around for 20 years, some operational people are still more comfortable with the original 13 fuel models. The original 13 fire behavior fuel models (Anderson, 1982), https://www.fs.usda.gov/rm/pubs_int/int_gtr122.pdf: * Represent wildfire behavior under peak fire conditions with cured herbaceous fuels. * Are sensitive to live fuel moisture in only five of the models, with substantial response predominately in fuel models 4 and 5;

fuel models (Anderson, 1982), https://www.fs.usda.gov/rm/pubs_int/int_gtr122.pdf: * Represent wildfire behavior under peak fire conditions with cured herbaceous fuels. * Are sensitive to live fuel moisture in only five of the models, with substantial response predominately in fuel models 4 and 5; none are dynamic. * Were created before crown fire modeling existed, requiring several models (fuel models 4, 6, and 7) to approximate crown fire behavior. See Active Crown Fire Behavior for more information. On the other hand, the 40 standard fuel models (Scott and Burgan, 2005), https://www.fs.usda.gov/rm/pubs/rmrs_gtr153.pdf: * Support analyses for fire use and fuel modification treatments. * Represent green, growing season conditions and cured, peak season conditions. * Incorporate dynamic fuel load transfer in some of the models, allowing behavior to shift with changing conditions. * Handle live herbaceous fuel moisture much differently. The most important benefit of integrating both fuel model sets is that users familiar with the original 13 can transition to the expanded model set, effectively providing a "dual language" guide. Dynamic and Proportional Fuel Load Transfer The NFDRS introduced the concept that most herbaceous fuels transition from green to cured conditions over the course of a fire season. As live herbaceous fuel cures, its load transfers into the dead category, redefining the fuel complex with each proportion transferred, making it a critical fuel model characteristic-particularly compared with the static fuel models in the original 13. Topography Topography significantly influences fire behavior by altering fuel conditions, wind patterns, and heat transfer. These factors affect fire spread and intensity. Understanding these factors is essential for predicting fire movement and planning effective suppression strategies. Slope Fires spread more rapidly uphill because rising heat preheating fuels ahead of the flaming front. Steeper slopes accelerate this effect, and narrow drainages magnify this effect even more. Fire position on the slope matters; even on a constant slope, fires spread faster at the top of the slope than at the bottom of the slope, a phenomenon known as fire acceleration, making fire behavior prediction on slopes more difficult. A fire starting at the top of a slope cannot readily take advantage of the steepness except when burning debris rolls downhill and ignites fire below. Slope reversals, such as when a fire crosses a drainage and transitions from a backing fire to a head fire, can pose threats to firefighter safety. Strong upslope fires that burn to the top of a ridgeline can roll over the ridge with high intensity, creating lee-side vortices where fire quickly burns back upslope or laterally (Finney et al. 2021). There is much to learn and study regarding

fires that burn to the top of a ridgeline can roll over the ridge with high intensity, creating lee-side vortices where fire quickly burns back upslope or laterally (Finney et al. 2021). There is much to learn and study regarding weather and fire behavior in complex terrain, and fire behavior practitioners are encouraged to study more in publications specifically written for fire managers and fire behavior specialists (Werth et al. 2016, Vol. 1 & 2). Downslope winds often develop as the sun sets as slopes become shaded. These winds are shallow and typically weaker but can become significantly stronger and long-duration when combined over a larger valley extent. Inversions are common in mountainous terrain. As cold air drains into valleys, fire behavior may be suppressed at low elevations while higher terrain remains warmer with lower humidities to support active nighttime fire behavior. Aircraft may be grounded if an inversion significantly affects visibility. When inversions break, a significant increase in fire behavior can occur. Anticipate inversions and adjust fire behavior predictions, strategies, tactics, and safety procedures accordingly. Aspect South- and west-facing slopes in the northern hemisphere receive more sunlight. This can dry the fuels, increasing fire intensity and increasing ignition likelihood.

Aspect South- and west-facing slopes in the northern hemisphere receive more sunlight. This can dry the fuels, increasing fire intensity and increasing ignition likelihood. Conversely, a very dry south aspect may have such sparse fuel that fire does not readily spread, and the more vegetated north aspects may have sufficient fuel to exhibit intense fire behavior. Elevation Lower elevations are generally warmer and drier and may support dry, flashy fuels that promote faster fire spread. Although higher elevations may slow fires due to cooler, moist conditions certain times of the year, they can also support heavier fuel loads that burn with more intensity and have higher resistance to control. The effects of elevation on fire behavior change throughout fire season and vary by latitude. Landforms Landforms, such as canyons, ridges, and valleys, can channel winds, funnel flames, and promote longrange spotting, leading to erratic fire behavior and rapid spread. More complex terrain, with more NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 96 of 205

vertical relief and diverse aspects over a large area, creates significant challenges for fire behavior prediction. Each combination of slope, aspect, fuel type, and wind pattern will result in different fire behavior and presents challenges in predicting fire behavior characteristics. Fuel Moisture Fuel moistures, for both live and dead fuels, can be determined through three primary methods: direct observation, physical sampling, and predictive modeling. Observed fuel moistures involve visual assessment by experienced personnel. These observations provide immediate, qualitative data useful for rapid initial assessments, though they can be subjective and lack precision. Sampling fuel moistures involves collecting fuel materials, weighing them, and drying them to determine their water content. This method provides highly accurate quantitative data but is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and represents only a single point in time that may not reflect conditions across a broader area. Modeled fuel moistures use meteorological data and other environmental factors to estimate moisture levels. These models offer continuous, spatially extensive estimates, which can be particularly valuable for long-term planning and real-time fire management decisions, but their accuracy depends on the quality of input data and the sophistication of the model and may not capture localized anomalies. Nelson (2000) developed a fuel moisture model for estimating the diurnal fuel moisture changes in a 10-hour NFDRS fuel stick. The model uses hourly weather observations to produce dynamic estimates that reflect changes in precipitation, humidity, and sunshine better than the Fosberg model. Their method, along with seasonal adjustment tables, was integrated into Richard Rothermel's (1983) field tools and methods for predicting surface fire behavior. Live Fuel Moisture Content Concepts and Methods Live fuel moisture describes the moisture in living plants and is categorized into herbaceous fuels (herbs and grasses) or woody fuels (shrubs and trees). Use Table 15 to assign appropriate live fuel moisture estimates and to interpret status of live fuels in the field. With the introduction of the Scott and Burgan 40 standard fuel models, herbaceous fuel moisture (HFM) is emphasized for fuel models that include herbaceous components. Importantly, HFM values below 120% indicate a dynamic transfer of herbaceous fuel load into the dead fuel category with lower fuel moisture. In contrast, the original 13 fuel models are intended for peak-season conditions and assume herbaceous fuels are cured and included as dead fuel. In NFDRS, live fuel moisture is estimated using the GSI, a weather-based index representing plant development. Growing Season Index (GSI) * The GSI (Jolly et al., 2005) quantifies environmental limits on plant physiological processes, particularly photosynthesis. It is highly correlated with seasonal changes in both the amount and activity of plant canopies, green-up predictions, senescence of live fuels, and the influence of water stress events on vegetation. The GSI integrates temperature, water, and light as the environmental drivers that regulate plant function. * VPD: High VPD increases atmospheric demand for moisture, causing water stress. Plants respond by closing stomata (partially or completely), reducing leaf development rate, inducing the shedding of leaves, and slowing or halting cell division. Although models are available to calculate soil water balance, they require knowledge of rooting depth, soil texture, latent heat losses, and precipitation. As a surrogate, VPD of the atmosphere provides an index of the evaporative demand without detailed modeling. * Photoperiod (or day length): Photoperiod provides a plant with a reliable annual climatic cue because it is consistent year-to-year at any location. Photoperiod sets the overall seasonal framework within which other climatic controls may dictate foliar development. Studies have shown that photo period is important to both leaf flush and leaf senescence throughout the world. More information on GSI can be found in FEMS: https://www.wildfire.gov/application/fems. Figure 50. Map of magnetic north across the U.S. Using Geographic Information Systems (GIS) Map Datum Maps use a datum to provide a consistent frame of reference for measuring locations on Earth. A datum defines the size and shape of the Earth (usually as an ellipsoid) and anchors the coordinate system to a specific point, ensuring accurate positioning across different regions and mapping systems. Without a common datum, maps from different sources could show the same location in slightly different places. * Common datums, or Geographic Coordinate Systems (GCS), used in North America include the North American Datum of 1927 (NAD27): a local datum well suited to the United States, Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean. Although largely replaced by NAD83, it may still appear in legacy topographic maps, historical land surveys, or older GIS data. * North American Datum of 1983 (NAD83): An Earth-centered datum that corrects NAD27 coordinates based on both Earth and satellite measurements. It is the most regionally accurate datum for North America. This is most likely encountered if using USGS topographic maps. Coordinates are similar to WGS84 coordinates (within 3 to 6 feet) and can be used interchangeably with them. * World Geodetic System of 1984

regionally accurate datum for North America. This is most likely encountered if using USGS topographic maps. Coordinates are similar to WGS84 coordinates (within 3 to 6 feet) and can be used interchangeably with them. * World Geodetic System of 1984 (WGS84): An Earth-centered datum common for datasets with a global extent. Uses the WGS84 spheroid. This is the datum that GPS coordinates are based on and will often be the GCS of files created during helicopter reconnaissance flights. Modern GIS software (e.g., ArcGIS) typically re-projects data "on the fly," but it is important to know why map layers may not be lining up appropriately, especially when using layers from a variety of sources in desktop software applications. Typically, if a shapefile is uploaded as a zipped file, the projection is included, which allows seamless reprojection. Consult a GIS specialist if datasets do not display correctly. Map Projections and Coordinate Systems As noted above, a datum defines Earth's shape and size and the origin point for a coordinate system. A map projection mathematically transforms the 3D surface of the Earth (as defined by the datum) onto a flattened 2D map. Examples are Mercator projection, Albers Equal Area Conic Projection, and Transverse Mercator (UTM) projection. Each will produce a different distortion, either in shape, area, distance, or direction. * LANDFIRE uses the Albers Equal Area Conic projection for national-level data. * WFDSS, IFTDSS, and FlamMap use a custom Albers map projection to preserve area accuracy and provide consistency across the US. For more information on using geospatial data in fire modeling applications, see the Fire Modeling section. A coordinate system defines how locations are measured and expressed on the Earth's surface using the datum (and sometimes the projection). There are two main types: * Geographic Coordinate System (GCS): Uses latitude and longitude based on the WGS84 or NAD83 datum. No projection is applied, so the coordinates are still 3D. * Projected Coordinate System (PCS): Uses planar XY coordinates in meters or feet and usually combines a datum with a map projection. Common PCS examples in fire management

NAD83 datum. No projection is applied, so the coordinates are still 3D. * Projected Coordinate System (PCS): Uses planar XY coordinates in meters or feet and usually combines a datum with a map projection. Common PCS examples in fire management include: * UTM: Divides the Earth into 60 zones that are each six degrees of latitude wide. When using UTMs, note the datum, such as, "NAD83/UTM Zone 12N." The UTM Zone cannot be adequately expressed without also knowing the associated datum. * State Plane Coordinate Systems: Units are projected based on the size and extent of each state. (Lambert Conformal Conic projections are used for domains with greater east-west extent, and Transverse Mercator projections are used for domains with greater north-south extent. Some states use an oblique Mercator projection). Figure 51. UTM zones for the CONUS. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 112 of 205

Observing Flame Length vs. Flame Height Flame observations help estimate fireline intensity and indicate tactical limitations. Accurate observation depends on distinguishing flame length from flame height. It is also important to identify whether the observation is from the head, flank, or back of the fire. Flame Length: The distance from the average flame tip to the midpoint of the active flaming zone at the base of the fire. When flames lean due to wind or slope, flame length is measured along the slanted flame angle. Flame Height: The average height of flames as measured vertically is estimated by comparing the flame to a nearby object of known height. Flame height is needed to estimate spotting distance from burning piles. Flame length is commonly used as a proxy for fireline intensity experienced at the actively burning perimeter. Flame height, on the other hand, is what most observers commonly report. Encourage observers to identify which measurement they are reporting and to use the appropriate definitions as described here. Surface Fire NWCG defines surface fire as: "A fire that burns surface litter, debris, and other loose material on the ground. Surface fires may spread by wind, rolling or tumbling of burning material, or by creeping along the ground; they may consume low vegetation and small trees but do not carry fire into the canopy." To estimate surface fire, assume this means within six feet of the ground. The intent of this section is to explain the fundamentals of surface fire predictions and equip personnel with tools and methods for predicting reliable surface fire behavior, enabling timely, informed, safety and tactical decisions on the fireline. When applying the Rothermel spread model, keep in mind that it assumes homogeneous fuels, steady-state conditions, and surface (non-crowning) fire; it does not simulate complex 3-D physics. Surface Model Inputs and Outputs The Rothermel surface fire spread model (1972) is a mathematical model that predicts the rate of spread and intensity of surface wildfires. It incorporates fuel type, moisture content, wind speed, and slope to estimate how quickly a fire will move across the landscape. The model is widely used in wildfire behavior prediction tools, including Behave, FlamMap, IFTDSS and WFDSS, and remains a foundational

incorporates fuel type, moisture content, wind speed, and slope to estimate how quickly a fire will move across the landscape. The model is widely used in wildfire behavior prediction tools, including Behave, FlamMap, IFTDSS and WFDSS, and remains a foundational part of fire science and operational planning. Here, the inputs and outputs are described to prepare for using tools that implement the surface fire spread model. Predicting Surface Fire Spread Using Lookup Tables Lookup tables provide a quick way to assess potential fire spread and flame length. However, they come with limitations and can only be used for rough estimates. Key considerations when using lookup tables: * Tables only reference the 13 original fuel models (Anderson, 1982). * Tables do not account for spotting or crown fire behavior. * The original 13 models were designed for peak fire season and are not well suited for shoulderseason conditions. * Outputs assume wind is blowing upslope, not across the slope or downslope. When wind is cross-slope or downslope, use a fire spread vectoring process (e.g., Behave), or use the Effective Wind Speed table with an input midflame windspeed (MFWS) of 0 mph for rough estimates. * The original 13 fuel models treat all live fuels (herbaceous and woody) as a single value. In Fire Behavior Fuel Models 2, 4, 5, 7, and 10, a live fuel moisture of 95% is assumed. If the current situation is significantly wetter or drier than this, the tables may not be useful. * Tables are valid only for slopes less than or equal to 25%. * Many tables show declining ROS and

Grass Fuel Models Fuel Model 1 (Short Grass - 1 foot) Fire spreads through fine, very porous, and continuous herbaceous fuels that are cured or nearly cured. Spread is rapid through cured grass and associated material; very little shrub or timber (less and onethird of the area) is present. Examples include grasslands, savanna, stubble, grass-tundra, and grassshrub combinations. Annual and perennial grasses are included in this fuel model. Fuel Model 3 (Tall Grass - 2.5 feet) Fire produces the highest intensity and highest rates of spread under the influence of wind within the grass group. Wind may drive fire into the upper heights of the grass and across standing water. Stands are tall, averaging about 3 feet (1 meter), but considerable variation may occur. Approximately one-third or more of the stand is considered dead or cured and maintains the fire. Wild or cultivated grains that have not been harvested can be considered like tall prairie and marshland grasses. Figure 58. ROS in Fuel models 1 and 3 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 125 of 205

Grass/Shrub Fuel Models Fuel Model 2 (Timber - Grass and Understory) Fire spread is primarily through fine herbaceous fuels-curing or dead-and through litter and dead/down stem wood from open shrub or timber overstories, which contribute to fire intensity. Open shrublands and pine or scrub-oak stands that cover one-third to two-thirds of the area may generally fit this model. Such stands may include clumps of fuels that generate higher intensities and may produce firebrands. Some pinyon-juniper are included here. Figure 59. ROS in Fuel model 2 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 126 of 205

Brush or Shrub Fuel Models Fuel Model 4 (Chaparral - 6 feet) Intense, fast-spreading fires burn through foliage and live and dead fine, woody material in the crowns of a nearly continuous secondary overstory. Stands of mature shrubs are approximately 6 or more feet tall. Flammable foliage and dead woody material significantly contribute to fire intensity. The height of stands qualifying for this model depends on local conditions. A deep litter layer may also hinder suppression efforts. Examples include California mixed chaparral, the high pocosin along the east coast, the pine barrens of New Jersey, or the closed jack pine stands of the North-Central States. Figure 60. ROS in Fuel Model 4 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 127 of 205

Fuel Model 5 (Brush - 2 feet) Fire carries in surface fuels made up of understory shrub and grass litter or forbs. Intensity is low due to light surface fuel loads-young shrubs, little dead material and limited volatile material in the foliage. Typical of short, green, nearly continuous shrub layers (e.g., laurel, vine maple, alder, or even chaparral, manzanita, or chamise) with no dead wood. Figure 61. ROS in Fuel Model 5 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 128 of 205

Fuel Model 6 (Dormant Brush, Hardwood Slash) Fire carries through the older or dominant shrub layers where foliage is more flammable than Fuel Model 5. Moderate winds (greater than 8 miles per hour, 13 kilometers per hour, at midflame height) are required; fire drops to the ground at low wind speeds or openings in the stand. A broad range of shrub conditions are covered by this model. Examples include intermediate stands of chamise, chaparral, oak brush, low pocosin, Alaskan spruce taiga, and shrub tundra. Even hardwood slash that has cured can be considered. Pinyon-juniper shrublands may be represented but may overpredict ROS except at high winds. Figure 62. ROS in Fuel Model 6 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 129 of 205

Fuel Model 7 (Southern Rough) Fire burns through surface and shrub strata with equal ease. Because live foliage and other live materials are highly flammable, fires can burn at higher dead fuel moistures than in other shrub models. Stands of shrubs typically range from 2 to 6 feet (0.6 to 1.8 m) high. Examples include palmetto-gallberry understory-pine overstory sites, low pocosins, and black spruce-shrub combinations in Alaska. Figure 63. ROS in Fuel Model 7 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 130 of 205

Timber Litter Fuel Models Fuel Model 8 (Closed Timber Litter) Fire is generally slow-burning ground fire with low flame lengths, though occasional "jackpots" or heavy fuel concentrations may flare up. Under most conditions the hazard is low, but severe weather conditions involving high temperatures, low humidities, and high winds increase spread potential. Closed-canopy stands of short-needle conifers or hardwoods that have leafed out support fire in the compact litter layer. This layer is mainly needles, leaves, and occasionally twigs because little undergrowth is present in the stand. Representative conifer types are white pine, and lodgepole pine, spruce, fir, and larch. Figure 64. ROS in Fuel Model 8 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 131 of 205

Fuel Model 9 (Hardwood Litter) Fire spreads through surface litter faster than Fuel Model 8 and produces longer flame height. This model includes both long-needle conifer stands and hardwood stands, especially oak-hickory types. Fall fires in hardwoods are predictable, but high winds can greatly increase the ROS more than predicted due to spotting caused by rolling and blowing leaves. Concentrations of dead and down woody material can contribute to possible torching of trees, spotting, and crowning. Examples include closed stands of longneedled pine like ponderosa, jeffrey, and red pines or southern pine plantations. Figure 65. ROS in Fuel Model 9 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 132 of 205

Timber Understory Fuel Models Fuel Model 10 (Timber - Litter and Understory) Fire burns in surface and ground fuels with greater fire intensity than the other timber litter models. Dead-down fuels- often including greater quantities of 3-inch (7.6-cm) or larger limbs- accumulate on the forest floor due to over maturity or natural events. These heavy fuels increase the likelihood of fire crowning, spotting, and torching, leading to potential fire control difficulties. Any forest type may be considered if heavy down material is present; examples are insect- or disease-ridden stands, windthrown stands, overmature situations with deadfall, and aged light thinning or partial-cut slash. Figure 66. ROS in Fuel Model 10 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 133 of 205

Slash/Blowdown Fuel Models Fuel Model 11 (Light Logging Slash) Fire activity is moderately active, burning in slash mixed with herbaceous vegetation. Fire potential is limited by light fuel loading, shading from overstory trees, or aging of fine fuels. Typical examples include light partial cuts or thinning operations in mixed conifer stands, hardwood stands, and southern pine harvests. Clearcut operations generally produce more slash than represented here. Loads of material less than 3 inches in diameter (7.6 cm) are under 12 tons per acre (5.4 tons per hectare), and fuels greater than 3 inches in diameter (7.6-cm) are represented by no more than ten 4-inch pieces (10.2 cm) along a 50-foot (15 m) transect. Figure 67. ROS in Fuel Model 11 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 134 of 205

Fuel Model 12 (Medium Logging Slash) These fuels can support rapidly spreading, high intensity fire capable of generating firebrands. Once ignited, fire spread is typically sustained until a fuel break or change in fuels is encountered. Slash is the dominant visual feature, consisting mostly of material less than 3 inches (7.6 cm) in diameter. Total fuel load is less than 35 tons per acre (15.6 t/ha) and seems well distributed. Representative conditions include heavily thinned conifer stands, clearcuts, and medium to heavy partial cuts. Materials larger than 3 inches (7.6 cm) are represented by encountering eleven 6-inch pieces (15.2 cm) in diameter along a 50-foot (15 m) transect. Figure 68. ROS in Fuel Model 12 under different effective windspeeds. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 135 of 205

Fuel Model 13 (Heavy Logging Slash) Fire is generally carried by a continuous layer of heavy slash. Large quantities of coarse woody material are present. While fine fuels comprise only about 10% of the total load, they carry the initial fires spread quickly, followed by building intensity as large fuels ignite. This model supports active flaming and a wide variety of firebrands, increasing spotting potential. Total fuel load may exceed 200 tons per acre (89.2 t/ha). Stands where the slash still has red needles attached but where total loads are lighter may still be represented, due to high early intensity and quicker area involvement. Figure 69. ROS in Fuel Model 13 under different EWS. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 136 of 205

Predicting Flanking and Backing Fire Behavior Figure 70 is a nomograph that uses EWS to produce adjustment factors for both spread rate and flame length. These factors can then be applied to the head fire behavior outputs to estimate flanking or backing fire behavior. Figure 70. Rates of spread for flanking and backing fire spread. 1. Find the EWS at the bottom axis of the right-hand chart. Draw a vertical line (a) upward to intersect the top axis. At that point, read the length to breadth ratio (b). 2. Determine the fraction of head fire ROS. From the same intersection point, draw a horizontal line (c) toward the left-hand chart, extending it until it meets the left axis (d) at the chosen spread of direction. Spotting and Crown Fire Spotting Spotting fire behavior is a specific situation where embers (firebrands) are lofted from the flaming front and are carried by wind ahead of the main fire front, igniting new fires in receptive fuels. Spot fires can significantly increase the spread and intensity of wildfire. Spotting is typically characterized as shortrange or long-range, though the breakpoint between the two is not universally defined. Additional information about spot fire modeling is available in Behave Help. Short-range Spotting occurs relatively close to the main fire and may not be significant for wildfire growth if the advancing main fire quickly overruns developing spot fires. Spotting distances of a few feet are typically represented in surface fire behavior modeling. Short-range spotting is usually 100 feet to 0.25 miles from the main fire front. Long-range Spotting differs from short-range spotting because firebrands are lofted by a convection column and carried beyond the immediate fire area. Long-range spotting is usually greater than 0.25 miles to several miles. In 2000, the Cerro Grande Fire was reported to have spot fires 10 miles ahead of the fire front. Figure 78. Evaluating spotting fire behavior requires three factors: * Source: Size, type, and number of firebrands based on source materials. * Transport: Lofting height and distance the firebrand is carried downwind. * Ignition probability: Likelihood a firebrand will ignite receptive fuels at the landing location. Estimating Maximum Spotting Distance Maximum spotting distance is predicted using equations developed by Frank Albini in the 1970s to estimate how far embers (firebrands) can travel and ignite new fires ahead of the main fire front. It considers: * Firebrand lofting height * Wind speed and direction * Topography (e.g., position on slope relative to wind direction) * Canopy height and tree species Although the maximum spotting distance is calculated, firebrands may land at all the distances up to that maximum. Crown Fire Definitions * Crown Fraction Burned (CFB) is a theoretical metric used to model and classify crown fire; it may be observable during post-fire burn severity assessments. It ranges from 0 to 1. * Passive crown fire (intermittent or persistent torching) occurs when surface fire intensity is sufficient to ignite tree crowns (individually or in groups) but winds are insufficient to support sustained crown-to-crown propagation; CFB is typically between 0.10 and 0.90. * Active crown fire occurs when surface and crown fire energies are linked; surface intensity ignites crowns and crown fire spread and intensity reinforce surface fire spread and intensity; CFB is typically greater than or equal to 0.90. * Independent crown fire (rare) occurs when crown fuel loading and flammability alone sustain fire without surface fire contribution under ambient weather and wind conditions; CFB generally approaches 1.0. * Isolated tree torching should not be treated as crown fire, although it may indicate future crown behavior during the burn; it usually results from local anomalies in surface fire behavior, terrain features, or brief wind gusts and corresponds to CFB less than 0.10. Crown Fire Initiation and Propagation In Conditions for the Start and Spread of Crown Fire, Van Wagner (1977), identified crown fire as the interaction between separate fuel layers in forested areas. He described two processes and defined models for estimating their potential. Crown Fire Initiation indicates the potential for a surface fire to ignite tree crowns and produce passive or active crown fire. Inputs include CBH and canopy FMC. The result is the threshold surface fire intensity required to begin canopy combustion. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 156 of 205

Active Crown Fire Propagation (crown spread) indicates the potential for continuous spread through the crown layer. Inputs include a characterization of canopy fuel density (single numeric value). The result is a threshold ROS required to sustain a solid crown flame with associated horizontal spread. These models are coarse because they represent highly variable characteristics (CBH and canopy fuel density) as broad averages; their inputs often require adjustment during modeling. Together, initiation and propagation models estimate when fires will remain on the surface, produce torching or passive crown fire, or progress to active crown fire. Fire Modeling with Spatial Tools Evaluating Expected Fire Behavior Understanding potential fire behavior and predicting fire spread requires a solid understanding of weather, fuels, topography, fuel moisture, and key fire behavior terminology-all of which are covered in this guide. Modeling systems and applications provide wildfire analysts with powerful tools for simulating fire potential across landscapes, but using them effectively requires analysts to: (1) identify and understand the problem to be solved, (2) choose an appropriate model, (3) select inputs thoughtfully, (4) interpret outputs correctly, and (5) validate results through field observation and discussions with local fire experts. Because no model can capture every real-world nuance, analysts must compare outputs with on-the-ground observations to judge accuracy. Landscape Characteristics Spatial fire models (FlamMap Basic, MTT, FARSITE, RANDIG, FSPro and FSim) require a landscape file (LCP or GeoTIFF). Dead Fuel Moistures Fine dead fuel loading and moisture generally determine day-to-day variability in flammability and responds to temperature, humidity, and precipitation. However, they may not reflect sufficient range in an analysis period to produce the observed variability. In FEMS, dead fuel moistures (1-hour, 10-hour, 100-hour, 1000-hour) are calculated with the Nelson (2000) method. Field estimates typically use the Fosberg method based on environmental conditions and charts. Typically, the Nelson method results in higher (wetter) values for fine dead fuel moisture than the Fosberg method. Understanding what application uses which method is important, for example, WFDSS retrieves fuel moisture directly from FEMS. In addition, when dead fuels are conditioned in FlamMap or IFTDSS for FlamMap Basic, MTT, RANDIG, and/or FARSITE, the Nelson method is used with the data from a weather file. To remedy this, a conditioning period (typically 1 to 7 days with an associated weather stream) can be set to allow fuel moistures to represent the range of local site conditions before calculating fire behavior characteristics. Conditioning periods can be set in FlamMap Basic, MTT, RANDIG, and FARSITE, but not in FSPro or FSim. Live fuels are never conditioned, and their initial values remain constant across a landscape for an entire simulation in all modeling systems. As the conditioning period progresses, the moisture content of the short time-lag finer fuels (1-hour, 10hour) adjusts to the local site conditions. The Nelson (2010) model is used to vary initial moisture conditions based on the spatial variation in topography and canopy cover, the weather file, and the length of the conditioning period. Because the short time-lag fuels (1-hour, 10-hour) have the most influence on surface fire behavior, longer conditioning periods generally produce little change when weather variability is low. Burn Period The NWCG Glossary defines the burn period as that part of each 24-hour period when fires spread most rapidly; typically, this falls between 1000 hours to sundown. When modeling fire behavior, the burn period is limited to when fire is actively spreading. This period may be shorter than the full window of observed activity. When considering the six categories of visual fire behavior (smoldering, creeping, running, spotting, torching, and flare up), all may occur within the 24-hour day. Field observers should be careful to report and describe their estimate of burn period accurately and purposefully and relate it to the type of fire observed: * Smoldering may continue around the clock for most active fires but does not indicate an active burn period if observed at the head. * Creeping may continue through the night but is generally transitional between smoldering and running fire behavior. Generally, it produces little overall fire spread and is not considered part of the burn period if observed at the head of the fire. * Running, torching, and spotting commonly

but is generally transitional between smoldering and running fire behavior. Generally, it produces little overall fire spread and is not considered part of the burn period if observed at the head of the fire. * Running, torching, and spotting commonly occur during the burn period when fire spread and overall growth are low to moderate. However, during peak hours, they may signal transitional fire behavior when more significant torching, spotting or crown fire occurs. Burn period length varies day-to-day: * Solar radiation heats fuels and reduces RH by warming the air which influences lower fuel moisture, creating conditions favorable for active burning. Slope heating is affected by the sun angle based on the time of year and latitude. Cloud cover and canopy shading can further reduce solar radiation. * Inversions limit solar radiation below the inversion layer, while heating continues above it, potentially creating a marked difference in solar radiation effects on a slope. Annual versus Perennial Grass Fine fuel loading associated with annual grasses shifts from live to dead and remains there for the duration of the season. Primary System Components and Indices Ignition Component (IC) The IC is a rating of the probability that a firebrand will cause a fire requiring suppression action. Expressed as a probability from 0 to 100, an IC of 100 means that every firebrand that contacts a receptive fuel bed will cause an actionable fire, while an IC of zero means none will. Note the emphasis is on fires that require action-not just ignition. Spread Component (SC) The SC is a rating of the forward ROS

Spread Component (SC) The SC is a rating of the forward ROS of a head fire. As Deeming, et al (1977), states, "the SC is numerically equal to the theoretical ideal ROS expressed in feet per minute. Highly variable from dayto-day, the SC is expressed on an open-ended scale; thus, it has no upper limit." Energy Release Component (ERC) The ERC is a number related to the available energy (BTU per square foot) within the flaming front at the head of a fire. Daily variations in ERC are due to changes in moisture content of the various fuels present, both live and dead. Since this number represents the potential heat release per unit area in the flaming zone, it can provide guidance to several important fire activities. It may also be considered a composite fuel moisture value as it reflects the contribution that all live and dead fuels offer to potential fire intensity. ERC is a cumulative, or buildup, index. As live fuels cure and dead fuels dry, ERC values rise, making

a composite fuel moisture value as it reflects the contribution that all live and dead fuels offer to potential fire intensity. ERC is a cumulative, or buildup, index. As live fuels cure and dead fuels dry, ERC values rise, making it a strong indicator of drought conditions. The scale is open-ended, or unlimited and, as with other NFDRS components, is relative. For example, an ERC value of 24 represents twice the potential heat release resulting in an ERC value of 12. As a reflection of its composite fuel moisture nature, the ERC becomes a relatively stable evaluation tool for planning decisions that might need to be made 24 to 72 hours ahead of an expected fire decision or action. Since wind does not influence the ERC calculation, the daily variation will be relatively small. The 1000-hour time-lag fuel moisture (TLFM) is a primary entry into the ERC calculation through its effect on both living and dead fuel moisture inputs. There may be a tendency to use the 1000-hour TLFM as a separate index for drought considerations. NWCG Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide 192 of 205

Note that any use of the 1000-hour TLFM as a separate index must be preceded by an analysis of historical fire weather data to identify critical levels of 1000-hour TLFM. A better tool for measurement of drought conditions is the ERC since it considers both dead and live fuel moistures. Burning Index (BI) The BI is a measure of the contribution of fire behavior to the effort of containing a fire. BI is derived from a combination of Spread and ERCs, producing a numeric value closely related to the flame length (in feet) multiplied by ten. The open-ended scale allows the BI range to adequately define fire potential, even in times of low to moderate fire danger. BI values represent the upper limit of expected fire behavior within the rating area. In other words, if a fire occurs in the worst fuel, weather, and topography conditions of the rating area, then BI values indicate expected fireline intensities and flame length. Although flame length is correlated with difficulty of control, containment is more directly related to fireline intensity-the rate of heat release per unit length of fireline (Byram 1959). Although flame length is correlated with difficulty of control, containment is more directly related to fireline intensity-the rate of heat release per unit length of fireline (Byram 1959). As BI increases, the difficulty of control grows at a rate greater than the increase in BI itself, though flame length remains a useful indicator because of its connection to intensity. Keetch-Byram Drought Index (KBDI) The KBDI is not an NFDRS output but is often displayed by the processors used to calculate NFDRS outputs. It is a stand-alone index that measures the effects of seasonal drought on fire potential. KBDI values estimate of the amount of precipitation (in hundredths of inches) needed to bring the upper eight inches of soil to saturation. A value of zero represents complete soil saturation, while the maximum KBDI value of 800 indicates extreme drought requiring 8.00 inches of precipitation to return to saturation. As KBDI increases, vegetation experiences increased stress due to moisture deficiency, and live fuels may become part of the dead fuel load through desiccation. Wildland Smoke and Air Quality Quick Guide for Smoke and Roadway Safety Smoke from wildland fires can drift onto roads and has contributed to serious and sometimes fatal vehicle accidents. While these incidents have occurred more frequently in the southeastern U.S., they have occurred across the country, and the meteorological conditions can occur in most locations, especially during fall. Nighttime Smoke Considerations The following conditions strongly indicate potential for nighttime smoke impacts on roadways: * Will there be active fire or smoldering within one hour before sunset and/or after sunrise? * Are there roadways within 10 miles of the fire? If yes, then nighttime smoke is a concern. If roadways are within 3 miles, these concerns should be deemed critical. * Can surface winds transport the winds toward nearby roads? * Can topography-such as drainages-channel smoke from the burn area toward any roadways? If the answer any of these is yes, then assess meteorological variables of temperature, RH, wind speed, and cloud cover. Probability Thresholds for Nighttime Smoke on Roads The NWS Weather Table, https://www.weather.gov/wrh/wxtable, allows a 7-day review of the four weather variables for a given location. Probability Thresholds for Nighttime Smoke on Roads The NWS Weather Table, https://www.weather.gov/wrh/wxtable, allows a 7-day review of the four weather variables for a given location. This helps determine whether more detailed roadway assessment of smoke risk is needed. When forecasted values show all four variables at critical threshold (Figure 108) there is a high probability of impacts from nighttime smoke. In these cases, additional analysis-such as running the PB Piedmont model, https://piedmont.dri.edu/-and mitigation planning should be considered. If the forecast includes a mix of moderate and critical values, further assessment and mitigation may still be warranted. In either case, coordination with IMET, Air Resource Advisor (ARA), Safety personnel, Public Information Officers (PIO), and local agencies (such as the state Department of Transportation and law enforcement) may be necessary to ensure proactive response and public safety. NWCG Incident Response Pocket Guide (IRPG) January 2025 PMS 461 NFES 001077 The NWCG Incident Response Pocket Guide (IRPG) establishes standards for wildland fire incident response. The guide provides critical information on operational engagement, risk management, fire environment, all hazard response, and aviation management. It is a collection of guidelines, checklists, and best practices that have evolved over time within wildland fire operations. The intended target audience of the IRPG is field-going wildland fire and aviation personnel from the Incident Commander Type 3 (ICT3) and Division/Group Supervisor (DIVS) level and down. The size makes it easy to fit in a firefighter's pocket, staying true to the purpose and intent. The IRPG does not provide absolute solutions to the unlimited number of situations that will occur. Some fireline decisions may be relatively simple; many are not. These decisions often require individual judgment, creativity, and collaboration - skills developed through extensive training, dedicated practice, and experience, which the guide facilitates. Operational Leadership The most essential element of successful wildland firefighting is competent and confident leadership. Leadership means providing purpose, direction, and motivation for wildland firefighters working to accomplish difficult tasks under dangerous, stressful circumstances. In confusing and uncertain situations, a good operational leader will: * TAKE CHARGE of assigned resources. * ASSESS SITUATION by gaining intel. * MOTIVATE firefighters with a "can do safely" attitude. * DEMONSTRATE INITIATIVE by taking action in the absence of orders. * COMMUNICATE by giving specific instructions and asking for feedback. * SUPERVISE at the scene of action. IRPG v

DUTY Be proficient in your job, both technically and as a leader. * Take charge when in charge. * Adhere to professional standard operating procedures. * Develop a plan to accomplish given objectives. Make sound and timely decisions. * Maintain situation awareness in order to anticipate needed actions. * Develop contingencies and consider consequences. * Improvise within the leader's intent to handle a rapidly changing environment. Ensure tasks are understood, supervised, and accomplished. * Issue clear instructions. * Observe and assess actions in progress without micromanaging. * Use positive feedback to modify duties, tasks, and assignments when appropriate. Develop your subordinates for the future. * Clearly state expectations. * Delegate tasks that you are not required to do personally. * Consider individual skill levels and developmental needs when assigning tasks. IRPG vi

RESPECT Know your subordinates and look out for their wellbeing. * Put the safety of your subordinates above all other objectives. * Take care of your subordinates' needs. * Resolve conflicts between individuals on the team. Keep your subordinates informed. * Provide accurate and timely briefings. * Give the reason (intent) for assignments and tasks. * Make yourself available to answer questions at appropriate times. Build the team. * Conduct frequent debriefings with the team to identify lessons learned. * Recognize individual and team accomplishments and reward them appropriately. * Apply disciplinary measures equally. Employ your subordinates in accordance with their capabilities. * Observe human behavior as well as fire behavior. * Provide early warning to subordinates of tasks they will be responsible for. * Consider team experience, fatigue, and physical limitations when accepting assignments. IRPG vii

INTEGRITY Know yourself and seek improvement. * Know the strengths and weaknesses in your character and skill level. * Ask questions of peers and superiors. * Actively listen to feedback from subordinates. Seek responsibility and accept responsibility for your actions. * Accept full responsibility for poor team performance. * Credit subordinates for good performance. * Keep your superiors informed of your actions. Set the example. * Share the hazards and hardships with your subordinates. * Don't show discouragement when facing setbacks. * Choose the difficult right over the easy wrong. IRPG viii

Communication Responsibilities All firefighters have five communication responsibilities: * Brief others as needed. * Debrief your actions. * Communicate hazards to others. * Acknowledge messages. * Ask if you don't know. Leader's Intent Additionally, all leaders of firefighters have the responsibility to provide complete briefings and ensure that their subordinates have a clear understanding of their intent for the assignment: * Task = What is to be done? * Purpose = Why it is to be done? * End State = How should it look when done? IRPG ix

Human Factor Barriers to Situation Awareness Low Experience Level with Local Factors * Unfamiliar with the area or the organizational structure. Distraction from Primary Task * Radio traffic. * Conflict. * Previous errors. * Collateral duties. * Incident Within an Incident (IWI). Fatigue * Carbon monoxide. * Dehydration. * Heat stress. * Poor fitness level can reduce resistance to fatigue. * 24 hours awake affects your decision-making capability like .10 blood alcohol content. IRPG x

Stress Reactions * Communication deteriorates or grows tense. * Habitual or repetitive behavior. * Target fixation - Locking into a course of action; whether it makes sense or not, just try harder. * Action tunneling - Focusing on small tasks, but ignoring the big picture. * Escalation of commitment - Accepting increased risk as completion of task gets near. Hazardous Attitudes * Invulnerable - That can't happen to us. * Anti-authority - Disregard of the team effort. * Impulsive - Do something even if it's wrong. * Macho - Trying to impress or prove something. * Complacent - Just another routine fire. * Resigned - We can't make a difference. * Group Think - Afraid to speak up or disagree. IRPG xi

Firefighter Stress Management Wildland firefighting is often stressful and sometimes traumatic. It can take a toll on mental health. It is normal to feel overwhelmed sometimes and it is vital to address these thoughts before they become a mental health issue. Mental fitness for duty is just as essential as physical fitness for duty. AWARENESS - Stress Injuries can be caused by: * A Life Threat: Due to an experience of death-provoking terror, horror, or helplessness. * A Loss Injury: A grief injury due to the loss of cherished people, things, or parts of oneself. * A Moral Injury: Due to behaviors or the witnessing of behaviors that violate moral values. * Cumulative Stress: Due to the accumulation of stress from all sources over time without sufficient rest and recovery. RECOGNITION - Stress Sizeup: Monitor yourself and others for: * Hazardous attitudes and stress reactions (see page xi). * Behavior changes (not talking, isolating, outbursts, increased use of substances, making mistakes). * Troubling feelings (fear, anger, anxiety, sadness, guilt, shame). * Thoughts or mention of self-harm or suicide. MITIGATION - Stress First Aid: * Shrink the stigma - talk about it! * Provide opportunities to calm: ○ Take a tactical

mistakes). * Troubling feelings (fear, anger, anxiety, sadness, guilt, shame). * Thoughts or mention of self-harm or suicide. MITIGATION - Stress First Aid: * Shrink the stigma - talk about it! * Provide opportunities to calm: ○ Take a tactical stress pause. ○ Refocus; identify what really matters. ○ Try tactical breathing or similar techniques. ○ Get additional time off if needed. * Get help: just like in a medical incident, a higher level of care may be necessary. * Reach out to friends, peers, loved ones, etc., for support. After Action Review (AAR) The climate surrounding an AAR must be one in which the participants openly and honestly discuss what transpired, in sufficient detail and clarity, so everyone understands what did and did not occur and why. Most importantly, participants should leave with a strong desire to improve their proficiency. * An AAR is performed as immediately after the event as possible by the personnel involved. * The leader's role is to ensure skilled facilitation of the AAR. * Reinforce that respectful disagreement is okay. Keep focused on the what, not the who. * Make sure everyone participates. * End the AAR on a positive note. What was planned? What actually happened? Why did it happen? What can we do next time? (Correct weaknesses/sustain strengths) IRPG xiii

Planning for Medical Emergencies Prior to each operational period, Incident Commanders (ICs), supervisors, and all wildland firefighters need to ask and be able to answer the following three questions: 1. What are we going to do if someone gets hurt? * Are there personnel on your crew/division/fire that can provide medical support? * What type of equipment is available to treat and transport injured personnel? 2. How will we get them out of here? * Could you get an injured firefighter to a road or helispot? * How many personnel and what kind of equipment would you need to get an injured firefighter out? 3. How long will it take to get them to a hospital? * Where is the closest hospital? * Will you use air or ground transportation? * Could conditions change and affect the transportation timeline? - Smoke/clouds/nightfall - Fire behavior - Mechanical failures All operational activities should be based on answers to these questions. If the answers are insufficient, stop, reassess, and consider alternate strategies and tactics. Reference Medical Incident Report, ICS 206 WF, on page 120.
